Ferdinand Magellan was a Portuguese navigator who led the first expedition to circumnavigate the globe, though he died before it was completed. He began his career serving the Portuguese crown in the Indian Ocean trade routes, but after a dispute with the Portuguese king, he shifted his allegiance to Spain. He proposed to the Spanish crown that he could reach the East Indies by sailing west, crossing the Atlantic and then an unknown ocean beyond South America.

In 1519, he left Spain with five ships and approximately two hundred and seventy men. He discovered the strait at the southern tip of South America, now called the Strait of Magellan, which allowed passage from the Atlantic to the Pacific. He named the Pacific Ocean for its apparently calm waters, in contrast to the rocky strait. He then sailed across the vast expanse of the Pacific without major sightings of land, and his crew suffered terrible hunger and disease. They called it the Gran Mar Desconocido—the Great Unknown Sea. He reached the Philippines in 1521, where he was killed in the Battle of Mactan while attempting to convert and colonize the local population.

Only one of his five ships, the Vittoria, returned to Spain in 1522 under the command of Juan Sebastián Elcano, with only eighteen survivors—but they had completed history's first circumnavigation. The voyage proved the Earth was far larger than previously believed, with vast unexplored oceans beyond the Atlantic.
